ranking.rationale: Workers in family is a strong, semantically stable proxy for household economic need and eligibility pressure for SNAP, and it should transfer better across domains than state/year/place-of-birth or demographic identity features.

Household presence/age of children is a strong, semantically stable driver of SNAP eligibility and need, complements work-status information already captured by WIF, and is less likely than state, year, race, birthplace, or citizenship features to encode domain-specific shortcuts.

Weeks worked in the past year is a strong, semantically stable indicator of household economic attachment and income insecurity, which directly relates to SNAP/food-stamp participation. It adds substantial signal beyond family structure already captured by WIF and HUPAC, while avoiding brittle domain identifiers like state/year and avoiding demographic shortcut features.

Usual weekly hours worked adds strong, semantically stable signal about labor-market attachment and economic need beyond weeks worked and work status already selected. It is broadly predictive of food-stamp participation across domains, while being less domain-identifying and less brittle than state, year, ancestry, place-of-birth, race, or other demographic shortcut features.

Educational attainment adds strong, broadly stable signal about socioeconomic status and SNAP eligibility beyond current work-intensity features, while being less domain-identifying and less brittle than state, year, race, birthplace, or citizenship variables.

Age adds strong, broadly stable signal for SNAP eligibility and need beyond household composition, work intensity, and education. It helps distinguish children, prime-age workers, and older adults without relying on brittle geography, race, nativity, or state/year identifiers.

Public health coverage is a strong, semantically relevant proxy for low income and program eligibility that should remain predictive across domains. It adds household-need information not already captured by age, education, family structure, and work intensity, while being less domain-identifying and less brittle than state, year, race, ancestry, or place-of-birth features.

Marital status adds stable household-structure information that is strongly related to SNAP/food-stamp need beyond age, education, work intensity, and household size. It is more semantically portable across domains than state, year, ancestry, race, or place-of-birth features, and less redundant than nearby labor indicators already partly captured by weeks worked and hours worked.

Worked-last-week status adds strong, semantically stable signal about current labor-force attachment and income insecurity beyond weeks worked and hours worked, especially for distinguishing unemployed or out-of-work individuals who are at elevated SNAP risk. It is more robust for OOD generalization than state, year, ancestry, race, birthplace, or other likely domain/demographic shortcut features.

Worked-last-week status adds strong, semantically stable signal about current labor-force attachment and income insecurity beyond weeks worked, hours, and class of worker. It is more robust for OOD generalization than geography, ancestry, race, or place-of-birth features, which risk encoding domain or demographic shortcuts.

Public health coverage is a strong, semantically stable proxy for low income and program eligibility that complements the already selected work, hours, education, age, marital, and household-size features. It is less likely than state, year, birthplace, ancestry, race, or citizenship variables to act mainly as a domain identifier or demographic shortcut, and it adds signal beyond the selected PUBCOV indicator by completing the binary recode.

Adds a direct, robust indicator of current employment attachment that is highly relevant to SNAP eligibility and complements hours/weeks/work-status features already selected; it is more stable across domains than geography, ancestry, race, or place-of-birth proxies and less redundant than adding another marital/education dummy.

Disability status adds strong, semantically stable signal for food-stamp need beyond age, education, work status, hours, and public coverage. It captures persistent limits on earning capacity and household need, while being less domain-specific and less brittle than geography, year, ancestry, race, or place-of-birth features.

Relationship to household reference person adds stable household-structure signal beyond household size, marital status, age, and work variables. Being the reference person versus spouse/child/other relative is semantically tied to SNAP eligibility and household economic dependency, while being less domain-specific and less shortcut-prone than state, year, race, birthplace, or citizenship features.

Adds the complementary disability-status indicator to the already selected disability signal, capturing a robust need-related correlate of SNAP participation that should generalize across domains better than geography, ancestry, race, or place-of-birth features.

Looking-for-work status adds strong, semantically stable signal about current economic hardship and SNAP eligibility beyond hours worked, weeks worked, and employment indicators already selected. It is more directly tied to labor-force distress than demographic or geography-coded candidates, while avoiding brittle state/year/domain identifiers and sensitive shortcut features.

Sex adds stable marginal signal for SNAP/food-stamp participation through labor-force attachment, caregiving, and household composition, complementing age, marital status, work, and children already selected. It is broadly predictive across domains and less likely than state, year, race, ancestry, citizenship, nativity, or place-of-birth features to act mainly as a domain identifier or brittle demographic shortcut.

Layoff status adds stable, policy-relevant labor-market hardship signal beyond current work, weeks, and hours already selected. It should generalize better than state/year/place-of-birth or race proxies and is less redundant than adding more marital, education, or relationship dummies.

Relationship-to-householder as biological/adopted child adds stable household-structure signal for SNAP eligibility and need beyond household size, marital status, age, and work variables. It is more semantically portable than state/year/place-of-birth/race proxies and less redundant than additional work-status or education dummies.

Spouse relationship adds stable household-structure signal beyond householder and child indicators already selected. It is semantically tied to SNAP eligibility and resource sharing, improving family composition modeling without relying on brittle geography, race, ancestry, or place-of-birth proxies.

Adds complementary marital-status information beyond married/not-married, helping distinguish widowed/divorced/separated households with different food-stamp risk. This is broadly stable across domains and less brittle than geography, ancestry, race, citizenship, or place-of-birth features.

Recent childbirth is a stable marker of increased household need and often co-occurs with young children, which strongly affects food-stamp eligibility and demand. It adds family-composition signal not yet captured by spouse/child relationship and household-size features, while avoiding brittle geography, year, race, or birthplace proxies.

Adds robust signal for being out of the labor force or unemployed via occupation not applicable, complementing work-status, hours, and weeks features already chosen. This is closely tied to SNAP eligibility through weak labor-market attachment, while being less domain-identifying and less brittle than state, year, race, ancestry, or place-of-birth features.

A higher educational-attainment indicator adds strong, semantically stable signal for food-stamp participation beyond age, work intensity, marital status, and disability. Education is a robust proxy for long-run earning capacity and economic vulnerability across domains, while being less domain-identifying and less brittle than state, year, race, ancestry, citizenship, or place-of-birth features.

Race remains a broadly stable correlate of SNAP/food-stamp participation through structural inequality and socioeconomic stratification, and it adds substantial signal not yet captured by work, education, age, marital status, disability, and household composition. It is less direct domain-ID leakage than state/year/place-of-birth features, and likely offers more marginal value than additional one-hot levels of already-partially-selected variables.

Adds a robust unemployment signal beyond current work-hours and job-search features. Being out of work is strongly and semantically linked to food-stamp participation across domains, while avoiding brittle geographic identifiers and more sensitive ancestry/place-of-birth shortcuts.

Adds hearing-disability information, a stable indicator of functional limitation and economic vulnerability relevant to SNAP participation, while avoiding brittle geography/year identifiers and offering complementary signal beyond the already selected general disability and work-status features.

Adds a broadly stable disability signal not yet captured: hearing difficulty is strongly associated with reduced work capacity and economic hardship relevant to SNAP participation, and is less domain-specific than geography, ancestry, place-of-birth, or survey-year features. It complements existing work, age, education, and other disability indicators with low leakage risk.

Cognitive difficulty adds stable signal about functional limitation and economic vulnerability that is strongly related to SNAP/food-stamp receipt, while being less domain-specific than geography, year, ancestry, or place-of-birth features. It complements already selected hearing and ambulatory disability indicators without relying on brittle demographic shortcuts.

Adds the complementary cognitive-difficulty indicator, which is a stable proxy for work limitations and economic vulnerability relevant to SNAP participation. It has strong semantic signal across domains and is less domain-specific or leakage-prone than geography, year, birthplace, or citizenship features.

Vision difficulty adds stable signal about functional limitation and economic vulnerability relevant to SNAP participation, complementing already selected hearing/cognitive/ambulatory/self-care disability indicators without relying on state, year, or birthplace proxies.

Completes the vision-difficulty signal already partially represented by DEYE_01; disability status is a stable, semantically relevant correlate of food-stamp participation and adds more robust household hardship information than domain-heavy geography, nativity, ancestry, or place-of-birth features.

Adds a strong, semantically stable education signal beyond the already chosen low-education and graduate-degree indicators: some-college/associate attainment helps separate working-poor households from both very low-education and BA+ groups, which is highly relevant for SNAP eligibility and less domain-specific than state, year, birthplace, or citizenship proxies.

Adds household-structure signal not yet covered by current RELP indicators: stepchild status is a stable proxy for complex family composition and dependent burden, which is strongly relevant to SNAP/food-stamp eligibility and need. It is more semantically portable across domains than state/year/place-of-birth features and less redundant than adding more education or marital dummies.

Adds a still-unselected household-structure signal: adopted child relationship. SNAP/food-stamp eligibility and need depend strongly on dependent children and family composition, and this is more semantically stable across domains than geography, survey year, birthplace, or citizenship proxies. It complements already selected spouse/biological child/stepchild/reference-person indicators with low leakage risk.

Adds household-structure signal not yet covered: this RELP category captures extended-family composition associated with SNAP eligibility/need, and is more semantically stable across domains than state, year, birthplace, ancestry, or citizenship proxies.

Recent childbirth is a stable, semantically relevant indicator of household need and SNAP eligibility pressure, adding family-burden signal beyond marital status, household composition, age, sex, and current work variables. It is more transportable than state, year, birthplace, or ancestry features and less redundant than adding more already-partially-covered relationship or education dummies.

Completes the fertility signal already partially captured by FER_00 and FER_02. Recent childbirth is a stable, semantically relevant indicator of household need and SNAP eligibility pressure, adding useful family-composition information without relying on explicit geography, year, or highly domain-specific origin features.

Separated marital status adds stable household-structure and economic-strain signal beyond married/widowed/divorced already encoded, and is more semantically predictive for SNAP participation than geography-, nativity-, ancestry-, or place-of-birth features that risk domain shortcutting.

Adds a still-missing marital-status category (divorced), which is a stable household-structure signal for SNAP/food-stamp participation and complements already selected spouse/children/fertility and other MAR indicators without relying on domain-identifying geography or year features.

Nativity adds broad, semantically stable information about immigrant status that is plausibly linked to SNAP eligibility and take-up through labor-market position, household resources, and program access. It is less brittle than state/year/place-of-birth indicators and more general than finer citizenship or ancestry categories, while still contributing signal not fully captured by age, education, work, race, marital status, and disability already selected.

Completes the nativity signal already started with NATIVITY_01 and adds a broadly stable indicator of foreign-born status, which is semantically linked to SNAP eligibility and take-up through labor market position and household resources, while being less domain-specific and less brittle than state, year, place-of-birth, ancestry, or citizenship-detail features.

English proficiency adds stable socioeconomic signal beyond nativity, education, and work status, capturing labor-market access and immigrant integration that are strongly related to food-stamp participation. It is more semantically portable than state, year, place-of-birth, or ancestry features, which are more likely to encode domain shifts or demographic shortcuts.

Adds meaningful signal beyond nativity and ENG_00 by distinguishing strong English proficiency from the baseline, which is plausibly and stably related to SNAP/food-stamp participation through labor-market access and program navigation, while avoiding direct domain identifiers like state/year or brittle birthplace categories.

Adds the remaining informative English-proficiency level beyond the already selected baseline categories; limited English ability is a stable, semantically relevant correlate of SNAP/food-stamp participation through labor-market access and household need, while being less domain-specific than state, year, or birthplace indicators.

Adds the remaining marital-status category (separated), which is a stable household-structure and economic-strain signal for SNAP eligibility/use. It complements already selected marriage and relationship features without relying on state/year/domain identifiers or highly brittle birthplace/ancestry proxies.

Adds the strongest remaining stable signal from English proficiency: inability to speak English at all is a robust indicator of economic and administrative barriers linked to SNAP participation, and it complements already selected nativity/citizenship-adjacent and work features without relying on explicit geographic domain identifiers.

Adds low-education signal beyond the already selected SCHL extremes; educational attainment is a robust, semantically causal correlate of food-stamp eligibility and need across domains, unlike state/year/place-of-birth features that mainly encode domain shifts.

Adds the strongest remaining stable signal about limited English proficiency, which is plausibly linked to SNAP/food-stamp participation through labor-market access and eligibility/navigation barriers. It complements already selected nativity and other ENG categories while avoiding brittle state/year/place-of-birth identifiers and weaker ancestry proxies.

Citizenship status, especially non-citizen vs citizen, adds stable signal for SNAP eligibility and take-up through access barriers, labor-market precarity, and household resource constraints. It complements already selected nativity and English features without relying on explicit geography or year identifiers, and is less brittle than state/place-of-birth indicators.

Adds the complementary 'not on layoff' signal to the already selected layoff indicator, improving labor-force-status coverage with a stable, semantically relevant predictor of food-stamp need while avoiding state/year/domain identifiers and more brittle birthplace/ancestry features.

Adds the complementary 'not looking for work' signal to already selected labor-force features (worked last week, hours, weeks, layoff, looking for work=yes). This sharpens employment instability and low-income status prediction for SNAP while remaining semantically stable across domains, unlike state/year/place-of-birth features that mainly encode domain shifts.

Adds the remaining informative layoff-status category (did not report) to complete a labor-force instability signal already partly captured by work, hours, and unemployment features; this is more semantically tied to SNAP eligibility than geography, year, ancestry, or birthplace features, which are more domain-specific and brittle.

Adds household-structure signal not yet covered by the selected RELP categories: being a parent of the reference person often indicates multigenerational or dependent-support households, which is stably relevant to food-stamp participation. It is more semantically portable than state/year/place-of-birth features and less redundant than more schooling or citizenship dummies.

Adds a strong, semantically stable education signal beyond the already chosen low and high attainment indicators: bachelor’s degree status is broadly predictive of food-stamp eligibility through earning capacity and labor-market attachment, while being less domain-specific or leakage-prone than state, year, birthplace, or ancestry features.

Adds the highest remaining stable signal from educational attainment: an advanced-degree indicator strongly tracks long-run earning capacity and SNAP eligibility, complements already selected low/HS education bins, and is more semantically portable across states than geography, birthplace, or ancestry features.

Adds the remaining informative category of looking-for-work status, complementing already selected employment and labor-force features. This captures active job search, a stable indicator of economic hardship relevant to food-stamp participation, while avoiding stronger domain-identifier risk than state/year/place-of-birth features.

Adds low-education signal beyond the already selected high-school/college SCHL indicators; very stable for SNAP eligibility because lower educational attainment tracks persistent income and employment disadvantage without relying on explicit geography or survey-year/domain identifiers.

Adds low-education attainment signal not yet covered by the selected SCHL indicators. Educational attainment is a stable socioeconomic predictor of food-stamp participation across domains, and this category should contribute more robustly than state/year/place-of-birth or other likely domain-identifier features.

Adds low-education signal not yet covered by the selected SCHL extremes; very low schooling is a stable socioeconomic predictor of food-stamp receipt across domains, unlike state/year/place-of-birth features that mainly encode domain or demographic shifts.

Adds a still-missing low-education attainment indicator, which is a robust cross-domain predictor of SNAP/food-stamp eligibility and need. It complements the already selected high-education SCHL categories by capturing the opposite end of socioeconomic status, while avoiding brittle geographic/domain identifiers like state, year, or place-of-birth features.

Food-service occupation adds stable signal about low-wage, variable-hour employment linked to SNAP eligibility, beyond existing work-status and hours features. It is more semantically predictive and less domain-identifying than state, year, place-of-birth, or ancestry features.

Adds occupation signal beyond current work-status and hours features: education-sector jobs are stably associated with earnings and household resources relevant to SNAP eligibility, while being less domain-identifying than state/year/place-of-birth features and less redundant than more demographic-coded candidates.

A broad business-occupation indicator adds stable socioeconomic signal beyond current work-status, hours, education, and unemployment features. Occupation category is semantically tied to earnings stability and SNAP eligibility, while being less domain-identifying than state/year/place-of-birth features and less shortcut-prone than finer geography or ancestry variables.

Adds the remaining high-school/GED attainment bucket, a strong and semantically stable correlate of SNAP eligibility through earning potential and labor-market attachment. It complements already selected low and high education extremes without relying on state/year/domain identifiers or brittle birthplace/ancestry proxies.

Adds an important missing low-education indicator, which is stably associated with food stamp eligibility and need across domains. It complements already selected higher-education SCHL categories without relying on state/year identifiers or brittle birthplace/ancestry proxies.

Adds an important missing education level indicator from the middle/low attainment range, which is stably related to SNAP eligibility through earnings potential and employment quality. It complements already selected schooling extremes without relying on state, year, or birthplace proxies that are more domain-specific.

Adds an important missing education level indicator from SCHL, which is a broadly stable socioeconomic predictor of SNAP/food-stamp participation. It complements already selected low and high schooling categories by filling the middle of the attainment spectrum, while avoiding brittle domain-ID features like state, year, or detailed birthplace.

Adds an important missing education level indicator from SCHL, a broadly stable socioeconomic predictor of food-stamp participation. It complements already selected low/high education categories without relying on state, year, birthplace, or other domain-identifying features.

Adds a missing mid-level education category, which is a stable socioeconomic predictor of SNAP/food-stamp participation across domains. It complements already selected low and high SCHL indicators better than state, year, birthplace, ancestry, or citizenship features, which are more likely to encode domain shifts or demographic shortcuts.

Adds an important missing middle education category, which is a stable socioeconomic predictor of SNAP/food-stamp participation across domains. It complements already selected low and high SCHL bins without relying on state/year/location proxies or brittle birthplace/ancestry shortcuts.

Adds an important missing middle education category, which is a stable socioeconomic predictor of SNAP/food-stamp participation across domains. It complements already selected low and high SCHL bins better than ancestry, birthplace, state, or survey-year features, which are more likely to encode domain shifts or demographic shortcuts.

Adds an important missing middle education level, which is a stable socioeconomic predictor of food-stamp participation across domains. It complements already selected low/high SCHL indicators better than ancestry, birthplace, year, or state features, which are more likely to encode domain or demographic-specific artifacts.

Adds an important missing middle education level, which is a stable socioeconomic predictor of SNAP participation beyond the already selected lowest and highest SCHL categories. It should generalize better than state, year, place-of-birth, ancestry, or other location/proxy features that risk encoding domain shifts.

Adds an important missing education level indicator in the middle of the SCHL spectrum, which is a stable socioeconomic predictor of SNAP participation and complements already selected low and high attainment categories. It should generalize better than state, year, birthplace, ancestry, or fine-grained citizenship/location proxies that mainly encode domain or demographic shifts.

Adds an important missing mid-level education category, which is a stable socioeconomic predictor of SNAP participation and complements the already selected low and high SCHL indicators without relying on domain-identifying geography or brittle birthplace/state proxies.

Adds an important missing education level indicator with stable socioeconomic signal for SNAP eligibility; more robust and semantically relevant than state/year/place-of-birth features, and less redundant than many remaining occupation or relationship categories.

Adds the remaining education-attainment category, completing a highly stable socioeconomic signal already shown to be important for SNAP/food-stamp eligibility, while avoiding brittle geography/year identifiers and more domain-specific ancestry/place-of-birth shortcuts.

Military-service status adds broadly stable socioeconomic signal beyond age, work, education, disability, and occupation already selected. It can capture veteran/active-duty household circumstances linked to SNAP eligibility without directly encoding train/test domain like state, year, or detailed birthplace/ancestry features.

Adds a broadly stable indicator of veteran/former active-duty status, which is semantically linked to household economic vulnerability and SNAP eligibility beyond the already selected work, disability, age, and public coverage features. It is less domain-identifying and less brittle than state, survey year, ancestry, or place-of-birth features, and likely offers more marginal value now than additional occupation or relationship dummies.

Adds the remaining broadly stable military-service signal after MIL_01 and MIL_02. This captures a meaningful labor-force and eligibility-related distinction without relying on explicit geography/time identifiers or highly brittle birthplace/state proxies, and should provide more marginal value than additional ancestry, birthplace, or state dummies.

Adds a broadly stable indicator for never-served military status, complementing the already selected MIL categories and helping separate civilian adults from active-duty/veteran groups without relying on state or birthplace proxies; likely modest but more robust marginal value than domain-identifying geography features.

Adds household-structure signal via grandchild relationship, which is plausibly stable for SNAP eligibility and food-stamp need beyond already selected spouse/child/parent relations. It is more semantically relevant and less domain-identifying than state, year, ancestry, or place-of-birth features.

Grandchild relationship adds stable household-composition signal highly relevant to food-stamp eligibility and need, complementing already selected spouse/child/parent categories without relying on state, year, or birthplace proxies that are more domain-specific.

Adds household-structure signal not yet covered: RELP_10 (other relative) can capture extended-family/co-residence patterns strongly tied to food-stamp eligibility and need, while being more semantically stable across domains than state, year, or birthplace features and less redundant than remaining education or occupation dummies.

Adds remaining household-structure signal via a still-unselected relationship category, which is stably relevant to SNAP eligibility and need, while avoiding brittle geography/year identifiers and more shortcut-prone birthplace/ancestry features. This is likely more marginally useful than additional occupation dummies given work-status features already selected.

Adds remaining household-structure signal via child-in-law relationship, which can stably correlate with multigenerational/extended-family composition and SNAP eligibility beyond already selected marital, fertility, and other RELP categories. It is more semantically portable than state/year/place-of-birth features and less likely to encode domain identity than geography-heavy candidates.

Adds remaining household-structure signal via an unselected RELP category, which is directly relevant to SNAP eligibility and need and is likely to generalize better than state, year, ancestry, or place-of-birth features that mainly encode domain or demographic-specific artifacts.

Healthcare practitioner/technical occupation adds stable signal about earnings capacity and employment quality beyond current work-status, hours, and education features. It is more semantically tied to food-stamp eligibility than geography/year identifiers and less brittle than state/place-of-birth proxies.

Citizenship status adds stable signal about SNAP eligibility and economic vulnerability beyond age, education, work, nativity, and English proficiency. It is less domain-identifying than state/year/place-of-birth features and less brittle than fine-grained ancestry; among remaining options, being U.S.-born is the most broadly useful marginal distinction.

Citizenship status adds stable signal about SNAP eligibility and economic vulnerability beyond age, education, work, nativity, and English proficiency. It is less domain-specific than state/year/place-of-birth features and less brittle than ancestry, while complementing the already selected non-citizen indicator with a distinct Puerto Rico/territories-born category.

Citizenship status adds stable signal about SNAP eligibility and economic vulnerability beyond nativity, English ability, race, and public coverage. It is more semantically relevant and less domain-identifying than state, year, or place-of-birth features, and likely more useful than ancestry or remaining fine-grained occupation dummies at this stage.

Citizenship remains semantically relevant to SNAP eligibility and economic vulnerability across domains, and this missing CIT category adds useful signal beyond nativity/English/place-of-birth proxies while being less domain-specific than state, year, or detailed birthplace/ancestry indicators.

Adds occupation signal beyond current work-status and a few occupation groups already selected. Cleaning/maintenance jobs are stably associated with lower wages and economic precarity relevant to SNAP eligibility, while being less domain-identifying than state, year, or place-of-birth features and less redundant than more schooling or relationship dummies.

Construction occupation adds meaningful residual signal about economic stability and SNAP eligibility beyond current work-status, hours, and broad occupation indicators. It is more semantically tied to income volatility than ancestry, birthplace, year, or state features, which are more likely to encode domain shifts or demographic shortcuts.

Adds stable marginal signal via occupation type beyond current work-status and a few occupation groups already selected. Community/social-service style jobs can proxy lower wages and public-assistance eligibility without directly encoding domain identifiers like state/year or brittle birthplace/ancestry categories.

Adds remaining occupation signal with likely stable relevance to food-stamp eligibility beyond already selected work-hours/employment features; managerial/office/professional occupation categories can proxy earnings stability without directly encoding geography or survey-domain identifiers, and are safer than state, year, or place-of-birth features.

Health-related occupation adds stable signal about earnings stability and access to employer benefits, which is relevant to food-stamp participation and complements existing work-hours, employment, education, and disability features. It is more semantically portable than state/year/place-of-birth indicators and less shortcut-prone than geography-heavy or ancestry features.

Personal-care/service occupation adds stable signal about low-wage, low-hour, and precarious work linked to SNAP eligibility, complementing existing work-status and some occupation groups. It is more semantically predictive and less domain-identifying than state, year, ancestry, or place-of-birth features.

Occupation remains one of the most stable predictors of food-stamp receipt beyond hours worked, weeks worked, and employment status. Among remaining options, an engineering occupation indicator adds useful labor-market stratification while being less domain-identifying and less brittle than state, survey year, or place-of-birth features, and less shortcut-prone than ancestry.

After strong household structure, work intensity, education, age, disability, and some occupation signals are already covered, the best remaining stable gain is another broad occupation category tied to earnings stability and SNAP eligibility. This adds socioeconomic information that should generalize better than state/year/place-of-birth features, while avoiding the stronger domain-ID and demographic-shortcut risks of geography and ancestry variables.

Adds occupation signal beyond current work-status and a few occupation groups already selected. Entertainment/sports/media is semantically tied to earnings stability and job quality, which affects food-stamp eligibility, while being less domain-identifying and less brittle than state, year, or detailed place-of-birth features.

Adds remaining occupation signal that is broadly tied to earnings stability and job quality, which are semantically relevant to food-stamp participation across domains. It complements already selected work-status and other OCCP groups without relying on brittle geography, survey-year, or birthplace/state identifiers.

Adds remaining occupation signal that is broadly tied to earnings stability and job quality, which are semantically relevant to SNAP participation, while avoiding brittle state/year identifiers and more domain-specific birthplace features.

Managerial occupation adds stable signal about earnings potential and job quality beyond current work-status, hours, and education features. It is more semantically tied to SNAP eligibility than geography, year, ancestry, or place-of-birth indicators, which are more likely to encode domain shifts or demographic shortcuts.

Adds remaining broad occupation signal not yet covered by selected work-status and occupation categories. Occupation is semantically tied to income stability and SNAP eligibility, and this coarse category should transfer better across domains than state, survey year, or birthplace features, which are more likely to encode domain identity or demographic shortcuts.

Adds remaining broad occupation signal not yet covered by selected OCCP groups. Occupation is semantically tied to income stability and SNAP eligibility across domains, while being less domain-identifying and less brittle than state, survey year, or detailed place-of-birth features.

Adds remaining broadly stable occupation signal after work-status, hours, and education are already covered. Production occupations are strongly tied to lower and more volatile earnings and thus SNAP eligibility, while being less domain-identifying than state/year/place-of-birth features and less shortcut-prone than ancestry/location indicators.

Adds remaining broadly useful occupation signal with relatively stable socioeconomic meaning for SNAP eligibility, complementing existing work-status and occupation categories. It is more semantically predictive and less domain-identifying than year, state, or detailed birthplace features, which are likely to encode benchmark shift structure or demographic shortcuts.

Adds remaining household-structure signal via an unselected RELP category, which is semantically tied to SNAP eligibility and need and is likely more stable across domains than state, year, ancestry, or place-of-birth indicators that mainly encode geography or demographic shortcuts.

Adds remaining occupation signal with plausible stable relevance to food-stamp eligibility beyond already selected work-hours/employment features. It is more semantically tied to earnings capacity than ancestry, birthplace, state, or survey year, which are more likely to encode domain shifts or demographic shortcuts.

Occupation remains one of the strongest stable signals for food-stamp eligibility after work status, hours, education, and household structure. Among remaining candidates, this occupation category adds socioeconomic information without directly encoding test-domain identity like state/year features, and is less brittle than birthplace/ancestry indicators.

Adds remaining broadly useful occupation signal beyond already selected work-status and many OCCP groups. Production-related occupation is a stable proxy for income volatility and lower-wage employment linked to SNAP eligibility, while being less domain-identifying and less brittle than state, year, or detailed place-of-birth features.

Adds remaining broad occupation signal tied to employment quality and income stability, which is semantically relevant to SNAP eligibility and more likely to transfer across domains than year, state, or place-of-birth indicators. It offers more marginal value than additional ancestry/geography features while complementing the already selected work-status and occupation categories.

Adds remaining broadly stable occupation signal beyond current work-status and occupation groups. Scientific/technical occupations are strongly associated with income and employment quality relevant to SNAP eligibility, while being less domain-identifying and less brittle than state, year, or detailed place-of-birth features.

Transportation occupations add remaining stable signal about labor-market position and income adequacy for SNAP eligibility. This complements the already selected work-status, hours, weeks, and many occupation groups, while avoiding brittle domain identifiers like state, survey year, or detailed place-of-birth features.

Adds the remaining occupation category and complements the already selected work-status, hours, and occupation indicators. Military occupation can still carry stable information about employment structure and income constraints relevant to SNAP eligibility, while being less domain-identifying than state, year, or detailed place-of-birth features.

Adds remaining household-structure signal via an unselected RELP category, which is directly relevant to SNAP/food-stamp eligibility and need, and is likely more stable across domains than year, state, ancestry, or place-of-birth indicators that mainly encode geography or demographic shortcuts.

Adds the remaining relationship-to-householder category, completing household-structure information that is stably relevant to SNAP/food-stamp eligibility and need. This is more semantically predictive and less domain-specific than year, state, ancestry, or detailed place-of-birth indicators, which are more likely to encode geographic/domain shifts or demographic shortcuts.
